Auto Supplier ZF Reveals the High Revolution Electric Drive That Spins at 30,000 RPM
9 photos
Photo: ZF
As the world sinks deeper and deeper into the era of the electric car, the technologies that have powered the early iterations of these vehicles are rapidly evolving. Most of the research was until now focused on batteries, so that they can deliver more range and less range anxiety, but now electric motors and the associated hardware are becoming the focus of research and development.
Several important evolutions in this field have come to light in recent weeks, and we'll focus here on something called the High Revolution Drive. It is a piece of technology made by German supplier ZF , and designed to spin extremely fast, while being lighter and smaller than most existing hardware.
How fast does this thing spin, you ask? Well, ZF talks about 30,000 rpm, which is roughly double what most present solutions are capable of today. Despite this, the design is 25 percent smaller and about the same percentage lighter than the platform it is based on, ZF's Select, which normally spins at 18,000 rpm.
The company says that, on top of all of the above, the magnet mass has dropped by 50 percent, and the system is capable of 93 percent efficiency, even at high rotational speeds and with a high gear ratio.
The 3-in-1 electric drive comprises a two-stage helical cylindrical gear transmission with an 18:1 ratio to send torque to the wheels, and it plays in the 268-horsepower class. Torque levels are enormous, with ZF saying they stand at 3,500 Nm.
The Germans say they imagined the High Revolution Drive with specific applications in mind: high-volume passenger vehicles with drive outputs between 200 and 268 hp. It has been designed in such a way as to be able to be integrated into both 400- and 800-volt systems.
For these rides, ZF promises not only the same amount of power in a smaller (and subsequently cheaper) electric drive , but also an increased range for the electric vehicle it is meant to serve. We're not provided with the numbers that make it clearer what that means.
Because it is based on the existing Select platform, which is about to be integrated into a number of upcoming electric cars, and uses existing technologies, the High Revolution Drive does not require significant investments from automakers to be adopted.
It's likely it will be a while, though, before we get to see the ZF High Revolution Drive in action on commercial vehicles. ZF admitted it is already in talks with several automakers it does not name to produce the technology, but at the same time it adds that it doesn't plan to start making it before the 2030s.
As with all other innovations, we'll keep an eye on this piece of hardware and report back once we know more about it and its capabilities.
